activities.anchor: The profession's history explains both its caricature and its cure
activities.caption: scrub the milestones from press agentry to dialogue
activities.name: prHistoryTimeline

events.title: Lee's Declaration of Principles
events.text: the public deserves accurate information, the press open access — and his Pennsylvania Railroad derailment response showed candour could be strategy

events.title: Ludlow Massacre counsel
events.text: Lee's advice to the Rockefeller family showed that listening, even belatedly, beats silence

events.title: Crystallizing Public Opinion
events.text: Bernays writes the field's first textbook and teaches its first university course

events.title: 'Torches of freedom' walk
events.text: reframed cigarettes as women's liberation — engineered consent's power and its ethical peril in one campaign

events.title: Grunig & Hunt's four models
events.text: press agentry, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetrical — history read as a progression toward dialogue

activities.caption: find the faulty line — a 'what PR is' briefing
activities.name: prSpinSpot

config.prompt: One line of this briefing on PR and spin is wrong — click it:
lines: Spin that unravels is a crisis, and crisis response is the discipline's most scrutinised product.
The profession's hard-won lesson is that honesty is a strategy rather than a virtue tax.
The PRSA Code exists because the field's failure mode — misleading publics — destroys the only asset it manages.
Deceptive reframing is what the job is, and it usually works.
config.correction: Deceptive reframing is the profession's failure mode, not its method — 'PR' as whitewash is the caricature the showman ancestors earned, not the craft.
config.why: The caricature sticks because early press agents really did work that way; the modern discipline manages the control–credibility trade with honest communication.

activities.caption: file each function by the public it faces
activities.name: prJobsSort

config.prompt: The function family — file each job by its public:

items.label: placing newsworthy, accurate information with journalists
communicating with legislators to promote or defeat legislation
building and maintaining community and government relationships
maintaining trust with the financial community

config.why: The seventh job — crisis management — faces all of them at once, which is why it is the discipline's most scrutinised product.

activities.caption: fill the blank — what a release actually is
activities.name: prReleaseCloze

config.text: A release is a %%0%% of newsworthiness, not a guaranteed story, and newsrooms rewrite, query or discard most of what they receive.
config.hint: It is written in news style and offered to journalists — offered is the operative word.

config.prompt: A 30-second 2021 Super Bowl commercial cost roughly 6 million dollars with nearly 96 million viewers. Roughly what was the price per exposure?
config.why: About 6 cents — scale is astonishing and cost per contact tiny. What money cannot buy is the endorsement itself: audiences know the message was paid for and discount it accordingly.

activities.anchor: that any publicity is good publicity
activities.caption: true or false — the publicity saying
activities.name: prPublicityJudge

statements.s: Publicity is simply coverage you did not pay for, favourable or not.
statements.why: It is neither good nor bad by default — and it can turn against you overnight.

statements.s: Unpaid coverage of a scandal is the least controllable asset in the field.
statements.why: Nobody paid and the journalist could have stopped it — control is exactly what you lack.

statements.s: Responding well to bad publicity can build more durable trust than the bad coverage destroyed.
statements.why: What the saying gropes toward is a claim about crisis management, not about coverage being welcome.

statements.s: Early press agents disproved the 'any publicity' saying by refusing scandal coverage.
statements.why: They lived by it — publicity at any price, accuracy optional. The saying survives from them.

activities.anchor: An organisation never has one audience
activities.caption: pair each public stage with its case
activities.name: prPublicsMatch

config.prompt: One layoff announcement, three publics — pair each stage with its case:

pairs.right: employees unaware their division is exposed
staff who have read the rumour mill
the works council and the journalists covering the restructuring

config.why: Three audiences need three strategies, not one press release — a public becomes active when people recognise the problem, feel involved, and feel unconstrained from acting.

activities.anchor: Crisis communication is where all of this converges
activities.caption: walk the response — SCCT under pressure
activities.name: prCrisisBranch

config.root: SCCT (Coombs) matches response strategy to how much responsibility the organisation bears. Matching wrong is catastrophic.

start.text: Evidence shows a fatal product defect was known about internally. What does the organisation say?

choices.label: Deny responsibility
choices.feedback: A denial — or a legalistic shrug — meeting evidence of organisational fault: the famous catastrophic mismatch.

choices.label: Full apology, compensation, corrective action
choices.feedback: The match SCCT prescribes for crises the organisation clearly caused.

aftermath.text: The first hours frame every later story. Next decision: who hears what, and when?

choices.label: Employees hear before the news does
choices.feedback: Employees as a primary public — the workforce learning of its own company's trouble from the news is a wound paid for permanently.

choices.label: Speculate to fill the news gap
choices.feedback: Speculation exposed as false destroys the credibility you will need tomorrow — say what you know and what you do not.

settled.text: The message is centralised; the listening is decentralised — each public's channels monitored, feedback carried inward by the boundary spanner.

config.why: Read closely, crisis practice is the symmetrical model under duress: research what publics are actually saying, tell the truth, respect each public's stake, and count trust retained or destroyed.
